note: The reasons for the faculty not being in me ('seeing that it does not presuppose thought, and also that...') lost their connective.
replacement: 10. I find in myself, moreover, several faculties of thinking, each with its own special mode. I find, for example, the faculties of imagining and perceiving. I can indeed clearly and distinctly conceive myself as a whole without them. But I cannot conceive them without conceiving myself; that is, they require an intelligent substance in which they reside. For [in the notion we have of them, or to use the terms of the schools] their formal concept includes some sort of intellection. Hence I perceive that they are distinct from myself, as modes are from things. I notice certain other faculties too, such as changing place or taking on various figures. Like the preceding ones, these cannot be conceived, and so cannot exist, apart from a substance in which they inhere. It is very evident, however, that if these faculties really exist, they must belong to some corporeal or extended substance; for their clear and distinct concept contains some sort of extension, and no intellection at all. Further, I cannot doubt that I have a certain passive faculty of perception, that is, of receiving and recognizing the ideas of sensible things. But this would be useless to me unless there were also an active faculty, in me or in something else, able to form and produce those ideas. Yet this active faculty cannot be in me [insofar as I am but a thinking thing], seeing that it does not presuppose thought, and also that those ideas are often produced in my mind without any contribution from me, and even often against my will. So this faculty must exist in a substance different from me. In that substance, as I remarked before, all the objective reality of the ideas it produces is contained formally or eminently. This substance is either a body, that is, a corporeal nature that contains formally [and in effect] everything contained objectively [and by representation] in those ideas; or it is God Himself, or some other creature of a rank superior to body, that contains the same eminently. But God is no deceiver. So it is manifest that He does not send me those ideas directly from Himself, nor through any creature that contains their objective reality not formally but only eminently. For He has given me no faculty to discover that this is so. On the contrary, He has given me a very strong inclination to believe that the ideas arise from corporeal objects. I do not see how He could be cleared of deceit if they really came from some other source or were produced by other causes than corporeal things. Accordingly, it must be concluded that corporeal objects exist. They are perhaps not exactly as we perceive them by the senses, since sense perception is in many cases very obscure and confused. But at least we must admit that everything I clearly and distinctly conceive in them, that is, generally speaking everything included in the object of speculative geometry, really exists external to me.

note: Source's 'for' giving the reason mind alone discerns the truth was dropped.
replacement: 15. There are, however, many other beliefs that seem to be taught by nature but are not. They found a place in my mind through a habit of judging things without enough consideration, and such judgments can easily contain error. Here are examples. I hold that any space where nothing affects [or makes an impression on] my senses is void. I hold that a hot body contains something in every respect similar to my idea of heat; that a white or green body contains the very whiteness or greenness I perceive; that a bitter or sweet body contains the same taste, and so on; and that the stars, towers and all distant bodies have the same size and figure as they appear to have to our eyes, etc. To avoid any indistinctness of conception, I must define precisely what I properly mean by being taught by nature. I am using nature here in a narrower sense than the sum of all that God has given me. In that wider sense the notion takes in much that belongs only to the mind [which I am not referring to here when I use the term nature]: for example, my notion of the truth that what is done cannot be undone, and all the other truths I discern by the natural light [ without the aid of the body]. It also takes in much that belongs only to body and is not included here under the name nature, such as the quality of heaviness and the like, of which I am not speaking. I keep the term exclusively for the things God has given me as a being composed of mind and body. In the sense I have explained, then, nature teaches me to shun whatever causes me the sensation of pain, and to pursue whatever gives me the sensation of pleasure, and other things of that sort. I do not find, however, that it also teaches me to draw conclusions about external objects from these diverse perceptions of the senses, unless the mind has first considered them [carefully and maturely]. For, as it appears to me, discerning the truth in such matters is the task of the mind alone, not of the composite whole of mind and body. Thus a star makes no larger an impression on my eye than the flame of a candle does. Yet I feel no real or positive impulse that determines me to believe the star is not greater than the flame. The true account is merely that I have judged so since my youth, without any rational ground. Likewise I feel heat when I approach the fire, and pain if I come too close. But this gives me no ground for holding that something resembling the heat I feel is in the fire, any more than that something similar to the pain is in it. All I have ground for believing is that the fire contains something, whatever it may be, which excites in me those sensations of heat or pain. In the same way, there are spaces where I find nothing that excites and affects my senses; but I must not therefore conclude that those spaces contain no body. For I see that here, as in many similar matters, I have been accustomed to pervert the order of nature. Nature gave me the perceptions of the senses merely to signify to my mind what is beneficial and what is hurtful to the composite whole of which it is a part, and they are clear and distinct enough for that purpose. Nevertheless I use them as infallible rules for determining at once the essence of the bodies outside me, about which they can of course give me only the most obscure and confused knowledge.

note: 'err' loosened to 'go wrong' and the source's 'for' dropped before the sick-man reason.
replacement: 17. But we also fairly often err in what nature directly impels us to, as sick people do when they long for drink or food that would harm them. Perhaps it will be objected that such people are deceived because their nature is corrupted. That does not remove the difficulty, for a sick man is just as truly a creature of God as a healthy man, so it is equally repugnant to the goodness of God that the former's nature should be deceitful as that the latter's should be. Take a clock, made of wheels and counter weights. If it is badly made and tells the hours wrongly, it follows all the laws of nature just as accurately as when it does exactly what its maker wanted. Likewise, consider the human body as a sort of machine, built and put together from bones, nerves, muscles, veins, blood and skin. Suppose that even if it had no mind in it, it would still make all the same motions it now makes involuntarily, and so without the aid of the mind, [simply through the dispositions of its organs]. I easily see that such a body, if it were dropsical, for example, would naturally experience the parchedness of throat that is usually joined in the mind with the sensation of thirst. This parchedness would dispose it to move its nerves and other parts as drinking requires, so that it would worsen its illness and harm itself. And it is just as natural for a body that is not ill to be moved to drink for its own good by a similar cause. Now, with regard to the use its maker intended a clock for, I may say that it departs from its proper nature when it tells the hours wrongly. On the same principle, if I regard the machine of the human body as formed by God for the sake of the motions it usually shows, I may likewise have ground to think that it departs from the order of its nature when the throat is parched and drink does not help to preserve it. Nevertheless I plainly see that this second sense of the term nature is very different from the first. The second is nothing more than a certain denomination, which depends entirely on my thought, and is therefore called extrinsic: by it I compare a sick man and an imperfectly built clock with the idea I have of a healthy man and a well made clock. The first sense of nature means something truly found in things, and so having some truth.
